Theme

Kitchen, meals & drinks

alcohol noun

also alcoholic drink, alcoholic drinks, strong drink, booze, teetotal, I don’t drink alcohol

classical

Plaut. Aul. 2.6.6: tēmētī nihil allātum intellegō (Lewis & Short)
Hor. Ep. 2.2.163
Traupman 281

tēmētum, tēmētī n.

noun, second declension

alcoholic drink, strong drink

(vōx prīsca et poētica: Plaut., Cato; Hor., Juv.)

Any intoxicating drink, wine or mead (Lewis & Short). The everyday classical way to speak of drinking is simply vīnum (see wine); one who drinks none is abstēmius.

Other words

  • alcohol, alcoholis n. — alcohol, the substance (in drinks, for cleaning wounds)

    noun, third declension · modern · Traupman 70, 270; M-O s.v. alcohol: alcohol, masculine, from 1846

    For the substance itself, as in a disinfectant or on a label. Traupman makes it neuter, Morgan–Owens masculine (alcohol absolūtus); we follow Traupman. Neither marks the vowels, and we leave them unmarked.

  • abstēmius, abstēmia, abstēmium — teetotal, abstaining from strong drink

    declension · also used · classical · Ov. Met. 15.323: vīna fugit gaudetque merīs abstēmius undīs (Lewis & Short)

    Formed like tēmētum and tēmulentus (drunk); in Horace more generally sober, frugal (Ep. 1.12.7).

  • spīritus vīnī — spirit of wine: distilled alcohol, ethanol

    also used · modern · M-O s.v. alcohol

    The older chemists’ name, from 1826 in Morgan–Owens.

Examples

  • Vīnum nōn bibō: abstēmius sum.

    I don’t drink alcohol: I’m teetotal.composed

See also wine, drunk, hangover, beer.

SourcesLewis & Short: temetum · Lewis & Short: abstemius · Lewis & Short: spiritus

John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 70, 270.

Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio, s.v. alcohol.

The example sentences marked “composed” are ours.
